prompt: Why does this lesson call pinning the base of every move rather than an alternative to updating?

choices.text: Pinned packages receive security fixes from PyPI automatically
choices.why: A pin receives nothing on its own; that is the point of it.

choices.text: It makes every update a chosen, reviewed change
choices.why: Right. Floating versions update in production by accident; pins turn each update into a reviewed change.

choices.text: A pinned package is never affected by new advisories
choices.why: An advisory is about a version; a pin keeps you on it, affected or not.

choices.text: Replacing a package is impossible without a pin
choices.why: Replacement is about leaving a project, and needs no pin to do it.

prompt: `uv pip tree` on lesson 5's environment showed which package pulling in `packaging`?

choices.text: flask
choices.why: Flask's tree had six packages, and `packaging` was not among them.

choices.text: werkzeug
choices.why: Werkzeug pulls in markupsafe, not `packaging`.

choices.text: pytest
choices.why: pytest needs it too, but only in the development lock; the tree shown was linkbox's runtime.

choices.text: gunicorn
choices.why: Right: gunicorn 22 required it outright.

prompt: PyPI listed four gunicorn majors released after 22. What does that tell you about staying on 22?

choices.text: Version 22 is unsafe to run today
choices.why: A release history says nothing about advisories against 22; that is a different question.

choices.text: The project is abandoned and should be replaced
choices.why: Regular releases up to August are the opposite of abandonment.

choices.text: Each later jump will be larger
choices.why: Right. The further a pin falls behind, the larger the jump an advisory forces. A moving project is healthy, and the cost lands on whoever stays behind.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the tests pass on 22
choices.why: Passing tests today do not shorten the jump you will have to make later.

prompt: Match each situation to the move this lesson recommends.

pairs.left: a healthy project releases a supported version past your pin
a new package is added to the service
the maintainers state an advisory will never be fixed, and you sign with it

prompt: The first compile, run with lesson 5's `requirements.txt` still in place, kept `click` and `markupsafe` at their old versions. Why?

choices.text: uv keeps pins already in the output file if they still fit
choices.why: Right. A lock moves as little as possible, so a review reads only what moved.

choices.text: Newer versions of both were excluded by the date
choices.why: The clean compile with the same date picked newer versions of both.

choices.text: flask's range forbids newer versions of click and markupsafe
choices.why: The clean compile resolved click 8.5.0 under the same flask range.

choices.text: gunicorn 26 requires those exact versions
choices.why: gunicorn 26 requires nothing outside its extras.

prompt: What does a hash under a pin in `requirements.txt` protect against that the version number alone does not?

choices.text: A newer version being released
choices.why: A newer version has a different number; the pin alone already ignores it.

choices.text: A different file served under the same version
choices.why: Right. The installer refuses bytes whose hash is not in the lock.

choices.text: An advisory being published against that version
choices.why: A hash says nothing about advisories; it pins bytes.

choices.text: A dependency of the package changing its licence
choices.why: Licences are not what a hash checks.

prompt: `ci/test.sh` installs with `uv pip install --___`, so any package without a hash in the lock is refused.
A teammate edits `requirements.txt` by hand to bump one package and its hash, leaving `requirements.in` alone. What has been lost?

choices.text: Nothing, if the hash was copied correctly from PyPI
choices.why: The bytes may be right; what is gone is the guarantee that the lock is what the ranges resolve to.

choices.text: The image will be built from the network again
choices.why: The build still uses the downloaded wheels; the problem is in the lock.

choices.text: The lock no longer matches its header's command
choices.why: Right. Nobody can rerun the header's command and get this file, and the `# via` comments may now lie.

choices.text: `--require-hashes` will refuse the edited package
choices.why: It accepts any package whose hash is in the file; a hand edit passes.

prompt: Compiled with `--exclude-newer 2026-08-01`, linkbox's ranges failed. Why?

choices.text: PyPI refuses dates more than a month in the past
choices.why: The 2024 date worked for flask in the same capture.

choices.text: No gunicorn 26.2 had been uploaded by then
choices.why: Right. `>=26.2` cannot be met with files from before 24 August.

choices.text: flask 3.1.3 did not exist in August
choices.why: flask resolved to 3.1.3 at the October date; the resolver named gunicorn.

choices.text: A date without `--generate-hashes` is an error
choices.why: Dates and hashes are independent flags.

prompt: A malicious release of a dependency is published on Monday and removed on Wednesday. Your compile date is always a week behind today. On Thursday somebody updates the lock. What happens?

choices.text: The compile picks it up, because it was valid for two days
choices.why: With the date a week back, Monday's upload is after the date on Thursday.

choices.text: The compile never saw it
choices.why: Right. It is gone before the date passes it: the release lived inside the window the date excludes.

choices.text: The hashes catch it, since its file is new
choices.why: Hashes are generated from what the compile chose; they do not judge a release.

choices.text: pip-audit refuses it in the sca stage
choices.why: A fresh malicious release often has no advisory yet; the date is what kept it out.

prompt: What does the lesson name as the cost of a compile date a week behind?

choices.text: Locks become impossible to reproduce
choices.why: The date is what makes them reproducible.

choices.text: A fix published yesterday is held back too
choices.why: Right. That is the case for a written exception for one package.

choices.text: Every package must be downloaded twice
choices.why: The date changes which versions are chosen, not how often they are fetched.

choices.text: The tests stop running in the pipeline
choices.why: The tests ran against the dated lock in this lesson.

prompt: Put the checks this lesson applies to the gunicorn 22 to 26 update in the order it makes them.
items: read what changed in each major
see what it brings in or takes out
run the tests on the new lock
build and run the image in the pipeline

prompt: Lesson 8's Dockerfile, built with `--network none`, failed. What did that failure show?

choices.text: That Docker cannot build images offline
choices.why: The new Dockerfile built offline a moment later.

choices.text: That the old build fetched packages from PyPI during the build
choices.why: Right. The build depended on whatever the index answered, which nobody checked afterwards.

choices.text: That the base image had been tampered with
choices.why: Nothing about the base image changed; pip could not reach the index.

choices.text: That the wheels directory was missing from `.dockerignore`
choices.why: The old Dockerfile used no wheels at all.

prompt: How many wheels did `ci/build.sh` download into `wheels/` for linkbox's runtime lock?
Which of these are true of the build after this lesson? Choose every one that is.

choices.text: Each wheel is checked against its hash twice, before and inside the build
choices.why: Right: `pip download --require-hashes`, then `pip install --require-hashes` in the Dockerfile.

choices.text: Both base images are named by digest
choices.why: Right, with the tag kept in front for the reader.

choices.text: The build's RUN steps reach PyPI through the proxy
choices.why: `--network none` gives them no network at all.

choices.text: `packaging` is installed in the image for gunicorn
choices.why: Python's own check printed `None` for it.

prompt: The ecdsa advisory says signature verification is unaffected. A service only verifies signatures somebody else made. What does the lesson recommend?

choices.text: Replace it at once, because the advisory has no fix
choices.why: The text says the vulnerable operations are signing and key generation, which this service never does.

choices.text: Keep it pinned, with the reason written in the gate's exceptions
choices.why: Right. The advisory does not apply to what the service does, and the exception records why.

choices.text: Update to the latest release, which fixes it
choices.why: There is no fixed version; `fixed_in` was empty.

choices.text: Fork the library and patch the timing leak yourself
choices.why: That makes you the maintainer of a cryptographic library, the most expensive option there is.

prompt: A service signs a token only so that the same service can check it on a later request. Which replacement for `ecdsa` does the lesson argue for?

choices.text: `cryptography`'s ECDSA on the same curve
choices.why: It works, but a signature is more than the job needs; nobody else verifies it.

choices.text: A newer release of `ecdsa` with the timing fix
choices.why: The project stated there is no planned fix.

choices.text: `hmac` from the standard library
choices.why: Right, compared with `compare_digest`. One party creating and checking its own messages needs a MAC, and no dependency at all.

choices.text: A hash of the token with SHA-256
choices.why: Anybody can compute a plain hash, so it proves nothing about who made the token.

prompt: A team's lock is compiled without a date, and a nightly job recompiles it and commits the result. Which two properties of this lesson's lock does that give up?

choices.text: Hashes and the `# via` comments
choices.why: Both are still written by every compile, dated or not.

choices.text: Reproducing the file from its header, and the cooling-off period
choices.why: Right. Without a date the same command answers differently tomorrow, and a release from an hour ago gets in.

choices.text: The upper bounds and the lower bounds in `requirements.in`
choices.why: Those are in the `.in` file and the job does not touch them.

choices.text: The offline build and the base image digests
choices.why: Those live in the Dockerfile and `ci/build.sh`, untouched by a recompile.

prompt: After this lesson, how do you show that `packaging` is not in linkbox's image?

choices.text: Ask the image's own Python
choices.why: Right. `find_spec` printed `None`, from inside the image, with no shell needed.

choices.text: Open a shell in the container and run `pip list`
choices.why: The distroless image has no shell and no pip, by lesson 8's design.

choices.text: Search `requirements.in` for the word
choices.why: It was never in `requirements.in`; it came in through gunicorn 22.

choices.text: Check that `requirements-dev.txt` no longer lists it
choices.why: It still does, for pytest, and that lock never reaches the image.
